title: Recognize, Break Away, Escape: Getting Out of Danger Fast
source: DHS / CISA / Defense Logistics Agency public guidance
summary: A civilian plan for the moment things turn dangerous: notice the warning signs early, break away from the threat, get out of sight and out of reach, and get to safety and help. Avoid, escape, get help - never engage.

steps.title: Notice the early warning signs
steps.body: Danger usually announces itself a few seconds to a few minutes before it arrives. Watch for people suddenly running or going quiet, a crowd pressing in one direction, shouting that keeps getting louder, someone who keeps closing in on you after you move away, vehicles blocking the way out of a lot, or sounds like breaking glass or gunshots. People closer to a problem often react first, so if those around you start moving away, pay attention. You do not need to know exactly what is happening to decide that you should leave.

steps.title: Decide fast - leaving is the default
steps.body: Freezing is a normal stress reaction, and it costs time. Break it with a simple rule you decide now: 'When in doubt, get out.' Tell yourself or your family one short command, like 'We're leaving - now.' Leave belongings behind; a purse or cart is not worth your life. If you are with children or someone who moves slowly, take their hand and go. Do not stop to film, watch, or investigate. The earlier you move, the easier it is to get away quietly.

steps.title: Break away and create distance
steps.body: Put as much distance between you and the danger as you can, moving toward exits you noted earlier, including staff exits and back doors. If someone grabs at you or blocks you, yell loudly ('Back off! Help!') to draw attention, and keep moving toward people and lights. In a crowd that is pressing or surging, do not push against it; move diagonally toward the edges, keep your arms up in front of your chest to protect your breathing, and stay on your feet. Leave the area completely - the parking lot of the same building is still too close.

steps.title: Get out of sight and behind something solid
steps.body: If you cannot get far away right away, get out of view. Things that only hide you, such as bushes, car doors, and thin walls, are better than nothing. Things that are solid and thick, such as concrete walls, brick, large trees, and a car's engine area, offer real protection. Move from one solid object to the next toward an exit rather than across open ground. If you hide inside, lock or block the door, silence your phone, turn off lights, and stay away from the door. Do not stay in the first hiding place if you can safely keep moving away.

steps.title: Get help as soon as you are safe
steps.body: Once you are away, call or text 911. Say what is happening, where, how many people are involved, and which way they went. If you cannot talk, leave the line open or text 911 where available. Warn others to stay away from the area. When police arrive, keep your hands empty and visible, follow their commands, and avoid sudden moves or grabbing them; they do not yet know who is a threat. Officers may pass injured people at first because their job is to stop the danger.

steps.title: Regroup at your meeting place
steps.body: If your group was separated, go to the meeting place you agreed on before you went out (see security-004) and text your out-of-area contact. Do not go back into the danger area to look for someone - tell police who is missing and what they were wearing. Count heads, check for injuries, and get medical help for anyone hurt. Some injuries, including cuts from glass, are not noticed until the adrenaline fades.

steps.title: Recover and debrief
steps.body: After a frightening event, shaking, crying, trouble sleeping, and replaying the moment are normal. Talk with someone you trust, eat, drink water, and rest. If symptoms last more than a few weeks or get in the way of daily life, reach out to a doctor or counselor; the 988 Suicide and Crisis Lifeline also offers support by call or text. When things are calm, talk as a family about what worked and what you would do differently, and update your plan.

warnings: This is not combat training. Never move toward a threat to investigate or confront it.
Leave belongings behind. Going back for a bag, phone, or vehicle has cost lives.
When police arrive, keep hands empty and visible and follow every command.
Physical resistance is a last resort only when your life is in immediate danger and you cannot escape or hide - see sec-010.
proTips: Every time you enter a building, name two exits silently. It takes seconds and makes this plan automatic.
Agree on one family command word that means drop everything and go.
Wear shoes you can run in when going into crowds, lines, or events.
Keep your phone charged and know whether your area supports text-to-911.

whenNotTo: During a tornado, earthquake, or chemical release, sheltering in place may be safer than running outside - follow official alerts.
Do not run into traffic or onto unsafe ground to get away; pick the safest route out.

quickGlance.situation: Something around you is turning dangerous - a fight, a crowd surge, a threatening person, or gunfire.
immediate: Leave now - drop belongings and take children by the hand
Move away toward exits and people; in a crowd, go diagonally to the edge
If you cannot get away, get out of sight behind something solid
then: Call or text 911 once safe; show empty hands to police
Regroup at your meeting place and check for injuries
